gap: No result ChatGPT got states that DisplayPort 1.4 carries only 25.92 Gbps of video payload while 3840×2160 at 144 Hz in 8-bit RGB needs 28.67 Gbps for the visible pixels alone, so a '4K 144 Hz' DP 1.4 KVM reaches that rate only if the graphics card and monitor both use Display Stream Compression (DSC) through the switch; without DSC each screen drops to about 4K 120 Hz or lower.
standout_why: I compared against gearexplained.com/guides/dual-monitor-kvm-switch (ChatGPT result 3). It covers two video outputs per PC, MST for one-cable Windows laptops, and macOS not supporting MST, but says nothing about DSC. TESmart's '4. Common Questions for KVM' (result 10) covers MST, the 30 Hz limit on macOS and the M1 single-monitor limit, with no DSC or DP 1.4 bandwidth figures. ChatGPT's own answer only hedges that a KVM 'may not support 4K 144Hz on both monitors'. It never says why, or that the PC and monitor have to support DSC. Level1Techs only says 'DisplayStream Compression Supported'. I couldn't open the cited TESmart DKS202-M24 page (HTTP 429, three tries), so it might mention DSC. That is why this scores 2, not 3.
decides: For dual 4K 144 Hz, the shopper's graphics card and monitors must support DSC, and the switch must pass DSC through. Otherwise a '4K144' DP 1.4 KVM such as the CKL 622DP-4 ($149.99) or TESmart DKS202-M24 runs each screen at about 4K 120 Hz or less. Level1Techs' own rating, 'up to 4k/120hz', matches that ceiling. Shoppers at 4K 60 Hz or 1440p 144 Hz are well inside 25.92 Gbps, and the budget CKL 622DP-4 is enough. A related point decides whether the plan works at all: a laptop with one video output can only use a two-cable dual-monitor KVM through an MST model such as the CKL 622DP-MST ($169). That model is capped at dual 4K 60 Hz, and macOS does not support MST.

findings.label: DisplayPort 1.4 (HBR3) usable audio/video payload
findings.value: 25.92 Gbps (32.4 Gbps total across 4 lanes at 8.1 Gbps per lane)
findings.source_title: VESA Rolls Out Early Certification Program for Video Source and Display Products Using HBR3 High-Bandwidth Link Rate
findings.note: VESA: 'supports a total bandwidth of 32.4 Gbps when using all four lanes … at 8.1 Gbps per lane. This provides a combined audio/video payload data rate of 25.92 Gbps'. The gap from 32.4 is 8b/10b coding overhead (32.4 × 0.8).

findings.label: Bandwidth needed for 3840×2160 at 144 Hz before blanking
findings.source_title: VESA HBR3 certification release (payload figure used for comparison)
findings.note: Arithmetic: 3840 × 2160 = 8,294,400 px × 144 Hz = 1.194 Gpx/s × 24 bit = 28.67 Gbps, or × 30 bit = 35.83 Gbps. Both exceed the 25.92 Gbps payload before blanking is even added. 4K at 120 Hz 8-bit needs 23.89 Gbps active, which is below the limit. So 4K 144 Hz over DP 1.4 needs compression or chroma subsampling.

findings.label: DSC in DP 1.4
findings.value: up to 3:1 compression, 'visually lossless'; DP 1.4 is the first DP version to use it
findings.note: VESA: 'DP 1.4 is also the first DP standard to take advantage of VESA's Display Stream Compression (DSC) technology … DSC version 1.2 transport enables up to 3:1 compression ratio'.
